catalog_quote: In normal intonation (the affirmative of Voorhis) the primary stress and highest pitch fall on the second or the fourth syllable from the end of the word, the penult or the pre-antepenult. Pre-antepenultimate stress cannot be common in the world's languages, but as the final vowel in such words is devoiced perhaps the stress could be described as falling on the first or third from the end, counting only the stressable syllables. This devoicing is not found, however, in the word-final vowel sequences of the casual-style (5). Isolated words, as in one-word utterances or in lists, have the stress on the penult, as do words that have only two or three syllables: (7) nešakwe·némo̥ 'I was unwilling.' Otherwise, ordinary words in ordinary sentences typically have the stress on the pre-antepenult: (8) ... wa·wanéška·haki ... '... that you would go around with bad ones.' One sometimes hears unexpected primary or secondary penultimate stress: (9) ... nemečíme·nèmo̥, ... '... I hesitated, ...' The normal intonation is used for non-emphatic statements and commands and for question-word questions. In the interrogative intonation the utterance is spoken with a raised pitch (indicated here by an upward-pointing arrow) and the stress falls on the third syllable from the end, the antepenult. It is used for yes-no questions

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress (with highest pitch) is counted from the right edge and depends on utterance position: in citation/isolated forms and in all two- and three-syllable words it falls on the penult; longer words inside ordinary sentences typically carry it on the pre-antepenult (fourth from the end). Because the word-final short vowel is devoiced, Goddard notes this is equivalently 'first or third from the end counting only stressable syllables'. Under interrogative (yes-no) intonation the stress moves to the antepenult with raised pitch; the exclamative stresses and lengthens the final vowel. A host plus enclitic(s) is accented on the vowel immediately preceding the (last) enclitic (p. 163, 166).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Marked with grave accent; 'One sometimes hears unexpected primary or secondary penultimate stress' (p. 160); the exclamative has a secondary stress on the pre-antepenult (p. 161).
new_statements.exceptions: Interrogative, exclamative, vocative, emphatic and interjectional intonations each place stress differently (antepenult; final vowel; penult; penult or pre-antepenult); some interjections have lexically inherent final accent; enclitic strings shift the accent to the syllable before the enclitic; compound stems are accented like ordinary words (pp. 160-166).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level in citation (penult) but sentence-level in running speech (pre-antepenult); stress and pitch are described together as intonation patterns, and Goddard leaves open whether all are contrastive. Data from 1990 fieldwork at Tama, Iowa (speakers Adeline Wanatee, Leonard Young Bear); the author calls the observations preliminary.
new_statements.identity_note: Goddard 1991 describes Meskwaki proper as spoken at the Mesquakie Settlement, Tama, Iowa (1990 fieldwork), i.e. mesk1242; Sauk (Whittaker 2005, examined) is a separate Glottolog languoid and is not the basis of the statement. Jones 1911 is the same Fox variety (Tama) recorded a century earlier.

sources.note: No lexical tone is described; pitch is treated as predictable from stress, vowel length and sentence type: four pitch values (high, mid, low, falling-rising), the stressed antepenult high in all contexts, the penult low in statements and falling-rising in questions, unaccented long vowels low and short vowels mid. Word stress is antepenultimate in affirmative contexts and penultimate in interrogatives; the Sauk affirmative contour coincides with the Mesquakie question intonation described by Voorhis (1971:72). tone.quote: Word stress in Sauk falls on the antepenultimate syllable in an affirmative context and on the penult in an interrogative.17 There are four pitches: high, mid, low, and falling-rising, with the antepenult taking high pitch in all contexts. The penultimate syllable is characterized by low pitch in statements and by falling-rising pitch in questions. Long vowels not carrying the primary accent take low pitch and short vowels mid pitch. Interestingly, the question intonation of Mesquakie, which has been ably described by Voorhis (1971:72), coincides with the affirmative pattern of Sauk.
